response.sql:
WITH gender_counts AS (
  SELECT c.gender AS gender, COUNT(*) AS order_count
  FROM Orders o
  JOIN Customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
  WHERE o.date_order_placed > '2013-10-25 17:40:25'
    AND o.date_order_placed < '2017-05-24 19:26:44'
  GROUP BY c.gender
),
avg_count AS (
  SELECT AVG(order_count) AS avg_orders FROM gender_counts
)
SELECT g.gender, g.order_count, g.order_count - a.avg_orders AS above_average
FROM gender_counts g
CROSS JOIN avg_count a
WHERE g.order_count > a.avg_orders;

assumptions.assumption: date_order_placed is stored as text in 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS' form, so string comparison matches chronological order.
The inner join to Customers keeps only orders whose customer_id exists in Customers.
A NULL customer gender forms its own group and is included in both the per-gender counts and the average.
The average is taken over the per-gender counts (one value per gender group), not over individual orders.

alternatives.interpretation: Exclude customers with a NULL gender, so only genders 'M', 'F', or other non-null values are compared and averaged.
alternatives.sql:
WITH gender_counts AS (
  SELECT c.gender AS gender, COUNT(*) AS order_count
  FROM Orders o
  JOIN Customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
  WHERE o.date_order_placed > '2013-10-25 17:40:25'
    AND o.date_order_placed < '2017-05-24 19:26:44'
    AND c.gender IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY c.gender
),
avg_count AS (
  SELECT AVG(order_count) AS avg_orders FROM gender_counts
)
SELECT g.gender, g.order_count, g.order_count - a.avg_orders AS above_average
FROM gender_counts g
CROSS JOIN avg_count a
WHERE g.order_count > a.avg_orders;
